Vase with Cobalt-Blue Ground, Gilt Ornament and Landscape Panels

大清乾隆年製 — Dà Qīng Qiánlóng Nián Zhì · Imperial Cobalt-Ground Porcelain with Shan-Shui Reserves, Qianlong Period (1736–1795)

Cobalt-Blue Ground with Gilt Scrollwork Qing Dynasty · Qianlong 1736–1795 Jingdezhen Imperial Kilns Shan-Shui Landscape Reserves Turquoise Interior & Seal Mark Dronova GOM Method

Object Description

The examined vase is executed in a classical Qianlong-period court form: a tall cylindrical neck, broad shoulders, and a body that widens smoothly below — proportions consistent with ceremonial display vessels of the second half of the eighteenth century, combining monumentality with a controlled, elegant silhouette. The porcelain body appears thin-walled and precisely finished at the footring, on the evidence of the photographs supplied.

The vase's ground is a deep, saturated cobalt-blue overglaze enamel, over which an intricate gilt scroll ornament has been hand-painted: narrow gold key-fret bands frame the neck and shoulder, a geometric diamond-lattice diaper covers part of the shoulder, and a cartouche of gilt Chinese characters (partially legible, reading in part 富貴 — "wealth and rank" — within a ruyi-head-shaped reserve) appears at the base of the neck (Fig. 3). This combination of a rich monochrome enamel ground with fine gilt linear ornament produces a visual effect the accompanying notes compare to cloisonné enamelwork, a comparison that is reasonable as a description of the visual effect though the vase itself is painted porcelain rather than metal-bodied cloisonné.

Set within the cobalt ground are large white reserve panels painted in a shan-shui (mountain-water) idiom: layered, mist-shrouded peaks in pale grey-blue washes, snow-dusted pine and flowering trees, a small pavilion at the water's edge, and a tiny robed figure with a pack, walking beside the pines in the neck panel (Fig. 3). The landscape painting shows soft atmospheric gradation between foreground and distant peaks and a restrained, largely monochrome palette relieved by touches of green pine and reddish autumn foliage — consistent with the shan-shui literati painting tradition adapted to porcelain, as described in the accompanying notes, though this Atlas entry describes the visual character of the painting rather than asserting an attribution to any specific named court painter.

Technological Interpretation

The cobalt-blue ground shows, in the standard photographs, a deep, saturated tone and a glossy, homogeneous surface consistent with a well-fired overglaze enamel; the gilt ornament painted over it shows fine, controlled linework rather than a broad, uneven wash, consistent with brush-applied gold rather than a sprayed or transferred finish. The turquoise interior/base glaze is smooth and evenly toned in Fig. 3, without obvious pooling defects or discoloured patches.

Four magnified images were supplied for this object (see Microscopy below), specifically targeting the glaze/ground boundary near the rim, a pink enamel detail (likely from the landscape or a related decorative element), the cobalt reign mark itself, and a gilt line — a well-chosen set of zones for assessing exactly the claims made in the accompanying notes (natural cobalt diffusion at the mark, hand-painted gilding, layered enamel structure). The findings from each are reported individually below rather than folded into a single generalised claim.

Gemmological Optical Microscopy

Four magnified images were supplied for this object. None carries a scale marker, so all observations below are qualitative; the imaging device and magnification were not stated and cannot be independently confirmed.

Zone A — Glaze/Ground Boundary near the Rim

Close-up / Magnification unconfirmed

A pale, granular glazed field occupies the upper portion of the frame, meeting a near-black field below along an irregular, softly diffused boundary rather than a sharp mechanical line. This gradual transition is consistent with two glaze/enamel layers meeting and partially blending during firing, rather than one being applied as a hard-edged later addition — though the exact identity of the two zones (e.g., rim glaze versus cobalt ground) is inferred from context rather than stated in the image itself.

Zone B — Pink Enamel Detail

Close-up / Magnification unconfirmed

Rounded fields of a saturated pink-red enamel, showing a granular internal texture, are separated by dark, slightly raised contour lines against a pale ground — a texture consistent with fired overglaze enamel applied within a hand-drawn outline. This frame most likely documents a small decorative accent (e.g., a blossom) rather than the main shan-shui landscape, which is described in the accompanying notes as predominantly grey-blue in tone.

Zone C — Reign Mark, Cobalt under Magnification

Requested view — mark cobalt

A dense, dark cobalt-blue stroke — part of a character in the reign mark — sits within a paler, softly mottled white-blue glazed field. The pigment shows a feathered, irregular edge diffusing gradually into the surrounding glaze rather than a crisp, mechanically uniform boundary, and small sparkling inclusions are visible within the stroke itself. This diffusion pattern is consistent with underglaze cobalt applied to the unfired body and partially absorbed by the glaze during firing, which is the reading suggested for this zone by the accompanying notes; it is not, on its own, sufficient to date the object, but it is consistent with a genuine underglaze-blue mark rather than an overglaze or printed one.

Zone D — Gilt Line on the Cobalt Ground

Close-up / Magnification unconfirmed

A diagonal gold band with a visibly granular, slightly uneven metallic texture and a bright specular highlight crosses a dark cobalt field. The uneven, textured surface of the gold — rather than a perfectly smooth, uniform metallic sheen — is consistent with brush-applied gold fired at low temperature, as opposed to a modern sprayed, plated, or printed metallic finish, supporting the general reading offered in the accompanying notes, though pigment/metal composition cannot be confirmed without elemental analysis.

Diagnostic Checklist

  • Tall, broad-shouldered court form with a smoothly widening body
  • Deep, saturated cobalt-blue enamel ground with fine, hand-painted gilt scrollwork
  • Large white reserve panels with shan-shui landscape painting — misted peaks, pine, pavilion, figure
  • Gilt ruyi-head cartouche with partially legible auspicious characters at the shoulder
  • Smooth, evenly toned turquoise interior and base glaze
  • Underglaze-blue seal mark in a square cartouche on the base
  • Magnified image of the reign mark shows feathered cobalt diffusion into the glaze, consistent with genuine underglaze-blue application
  • Magnified image of the gilt line shows a granular, uneven texture consistent with hand-applied, low-fired gold rather than a modern metallic finish
  • Magnified glaze/ground boundary shows a gradual, diffused transition consistent with two fired layers meeting during firing
  • No elemental (XRF/SEM-EDS) data yet obtained — the conclusion should be treated as preliminary at the chemical level
The classical court form, the deep cobalt-blue ground with fine hand-painted gilt scrollwork, the shan-shui landscape reserves, the turquoise interior glaze, and the underglaze-blue seal mark together are consistent with high-quality Qianlong-period imperial porcelain of the type produced at the Jingdezhen kilns, combining the decorative richness of monochrome-ground enamelling with the literati aesthetics of landscape painting, as described in the accompanying notes. Of the four magnified images supplied, the reign-mark cobalt (Zone C) and the gilt line (Zone D) offer the clearest support for genuine, hand-executed underglaze and gilt technique respectively; the glaze/ground boundary (Zone A) and pink enamel detail (Zone B) are consistent with, but less specifically diagnostic of, hand production. None of the four images carries a scale marker or stated, independently verifiable magnification, so these readings remain qualitative. A conclusive attribution would additionally require elemental analysis (XRF/SEM-EDS) of the cobalt, gilding, and enamels, and a clearer, unobstructed photograph confirming all six characters of the base mark.
